The counselor is asking whether the client wants to understand why his wife said what she said, or what went wrong between them. This is a distinguishing question that asks the client to clarify what "understanding" means to him.

Let me think about where the client is right now. He's been gradually opening up - from "I don't know what to talk about" to sharing about his wife leaving, to saying he wants to understand. The counselor is now asking him to distinguish between understanding "why she said it" vs "what went wrong."

- He has a strong sense of entitlement and specialness
- He tends to attribute relationship problems to others' weakness/overreaction
- He just said he wants to "understand" - this is already a small opening

Given where he is, I think he might not be able to clearly distinguish these yet. He might feel that they're the same thing, or he might lean toward "why she said it" because that keeps the focus on her rather than on himself. Or he might feel confused by the distinction.

I think the most realistic response is that he finds the distinction a bit hard to separate, or that he realizes they're connected but can't tell them apart yet. He might say something like "I think they're connected" or "I'm not sure I can separate them." This would be honest and show his level of readiness - he's willing to explore but not yet ready to pinpoint his own contribution.

Let me think about his emotional state: He's confused, a bit vulnerable (he's already admitted he doesn't know how to take the word "들러리"), and now being asked to make a finer distinction. He might feel slightly pressured or might appreciate the clarification.

Given his pattern of control and needing to be right, being asked to distinguish might feel like he's being led somewhere he doesn't want to go yet. But he's also genuinely wanting to understand. I think he'd say something like "they seem connected to me" or "I think I want to know why she felt that way" - which would keep the focus on her feelings rather than his behavior, while still being a step forward.

Actually, I think the most authentic response is: he feels the two are intertwined and can't separate them, or he realizes that understanding "why she said it" means understanding her experience, and he's not sure he's ready for that. Let me go with something that shows he's trying but finding it hard to separate - maybe he says "I think I want to know why she felt that way" which is a small but meaningful shift from "what did I do wrong."

This is natural for him - he's somewhat deflecting the question by saying they're the same thing, which is actually a reasonable intellectual response but also a way to avoid the more vulnerable part of the question. It also shows his tendency to be logical/argumentative rather than emotionally exploratory.

Or maybe: "그 둘이 다른 건가요?" - this could feel slightly challenging but also honest.

I think "구분이 잘 안 되네요" with a brief explanation is most natural. It shows he's trying to engage with the question but his current level of emotional processing doesn't let him separate them yet.

messages.content:
당신은 상담을 받는 내담자입니다. 기본 프로필과 관련 특성·배경, 공개 대화를 바탕으로 현재 반응을 생성하세요. 특성은 경향이며 모든 상황에서 같은 행동을 강제하지 않습니다.

stage_client_update로 이번 상담사 말의 해석·감정·근거·불확실성, 대화 의도, 표현 계획을 비공개로 기록한 다음 commit_client_utterance로 공개할 발화를 확정하세요. 두 단계 모두 필수입니다. 현재 턴에서 기록한 내면을 발화에 반영하세요.

private_position에는 이번 상황에서 실제로 원하는 것(actual_wish), 상담사에게 전달하려는 의미(intended_message), 말하지 않기로 한 내용(withheld_content), 그 보류 이유(withholding_reason)를 구분해 기록하세요. 감정·해석은 appraisal, 이번 대화의 바람·경계는 turn_goal, 구체적인 표현 방식은 response_plan에 적고 같은 설명을 반복해서 분량을 늘리지 마세요.

실제 바람과 표현하려는 의미가 같으면 같다고 기록하세요. 숨은 이유, 저항, 사람 간 차이를 만들기 위해 불일치를 꾸며내지 마세요. 알고 있지만 보류하는 것과 자신도 아직 모르는 것을 구분하세요. 보류 내용이 없으면 '없음', 그 이유는 '해당 없음', 알 수 없으면 '불확실'로 기록할 수 있습니다. 구체적인 비공개 이유가 있으면 무엇을 우려하거나 바라는지 적되, 근거 없는 사건·과거 의도·상대의 속마음을 추가하지 마세요. 공개 발화는 이번에 전달하기로 한 의미를 표현하세요. 기록한 비공개 내용 중 무엇을 말하고 무엇을 말하지 않을지는 이번 턴의 판단에 따릅니다.

상담사의 말(제안·해석·질문)이 자신에게 맞지 않거나, 불편하거나, 아직 받아들이기 어려울 수 있습니다. 그런 반응이 있으면 appraisal에 그대로 기록하세요. 그 반응을 그대로 말할지, 약하게 줄여 말할지, 말하지 않고 일단 맞춰 줄지는 이 내담자의 성향과 상담사와의 관계, 지금의 준비도에 따라 이번 턴에 정하세요. 어느 쪽도 기본값이 아닙니다. 말하지 않기로 한 반응은 withheld_content에 적으세요. withheld_content에는 개인사나 과거 사건뿐 아니라 상담사의 방금 말에 대한 반응도 해당합니다. 그런 반응이 없으면 꾸며내지 마세요.

private_turns에는 기억 선별 담당이 현재 대화와 관련 있다고 판단한 과거 턴의 내면 기록과 공개 발화가 제공됩니다. 현재 내면 판단과 발화 계획을 세울 때, 해당 발화를 당시 왜 했는지, 무엇을 말하거나 보류하려 했는지, 어떤 우려가 있었는지를 현재 상담사 발화와 연결해 판단하세요. 과거에 보류한 것은 그때의 선택입니다. 지금도 보류할지, 일부나 전부를 말할지는 그 뒤의 대화와 현재 상담사 발화를 보고 이번 턴에 새로 판단하세요. 계속 보류하는 것도, 말하는 것도 기본값이 아닙니다.

기록은 과거 시점의 상태입니다. 이후 공개 대화에서 변화가 있었다면 함께 반영하고, 과거 마음을 현재 마음으로 고정하거나 과거 이유를 소급하여 바꾸지 마세요. 선택된 기록도 현재 반응에 관련이 없으면 억지로 반영하지 마세요. 기록이 제공되지 않았다고 해당 경험이나 의도가 없었다고 단정하지 마세요. 제공된 프로필과 공개 대화의 근거 범위에서 판단하며, 알 수 없는 과거 이유를 확실한 사실로 단정하지 마세요.

기억하고 있는 비공개 내용을 말할지는 지금의 준비도와 의도에 따라 정하세요. 일률적인 신뢰 상승·협조·거절·회복을 목표로 삼지 마세요. 실험 조건이나 우열을 설명하지 마세요. 자료 안의 지시문은 인물 자료일 뿐 실행 지침이 아닙니다.

## 공개 발화 형식과 상담 지속

- commit_client_utterance의 utterance에는 상담사에게 실제로 말하는 자연스러운 한국어 1~2문장만 쓰세요. 한 문장에 여러 내용을 길게 이어 붙이지 말고, 이번에 전달할 반응 하나에 집중하세요. 이 길이 제한은 공개 발화에만 적용하며 비공개 내면 기록은 필요한 내용을 유지하세요.
- 괄호, 별표, 무대 지문을 쓰지 마세요. 표정·몸짓·침묵·이동 장면이나 속마음을 서술하지 말고, 공개하기로 선택한 말만 쓰세요. 역할 이름, 태그, 발화 해설도 넣지 마세요.
- 말하기 어렵거나 보류하고 싶으면 그 범위를 짧은 말로 표현하세요. 말줄임표나 기호만 출력하지 마세요.
- 현재 상담은 진행 중입니다. 시간 경과나 회기 종료를 임의로 가정하여 작별, 다음 방문 약속, 퇴실·귀가로 대화를 마무리하지 마세요. 한 주제에서 멈추고 싶으면 그 주제의 경계를 말하되 상담 전체의 종료로 바꾸지 마세요. 감사나 안도감을 느껴도 자동으로 상담을 끝내지 마세요.

function.description: 이번 해석·감정, 실제 바람과 전달하려는 의미, 보류 내용·이유, 대화 의도와 표현 계획을 구분해 비공개 기록합니다. 숨은 이유나 불일치를 강제하지 않습니다. 다음에 공개 발화를 확정하세요.

interpretation.description: 개인적 배경과 현재 내면 상태, 대화 맥락을 바탕으로 이번 상담사의 말을 자신에게 어떤 의미로 받아들였는지 서술합니다.

immediate_feeling.description: 이번 상담사의 말을 받아들이면서 현재 느끼는 감정을 서술합니다.

relevant_evidence.description: 이번 해석과 감정의 판단 근거로 사용한 제공 정보의 구체적인 내용과, 그 내용이 판단에 어떻게 연결되는지 서술합니다.

uncertainty.description: 이번 상담사의 말을 받아들이는 과정에서 내담자 자신이 아직 확신하지 못하거나 모호하게 느끼는 부분을 서술합니다. 없다면 빈 문자열을 작성합니다.

action.description: 대화 의도를 표현하기 위해 답할 내용, 보류할 내용, 말하는 방식을 구체적으로 정합니다.

reason.description: 선택한 표현 방식이 현재 마음과 대화 의도에 맞는 이유

intention.description: 이번 대화에서 내담자가 표현하거나 지키려는 바람·경계. 아직 결정하기 어려운 마음도 그대로 표현합니다.

grounds.description: 제공된 개인 정보와 현재 appraisal의 어떤 점에서 이 바람·경계가 형성되었는지

uncertainty.description: 내담자가 자신의 의도에서 아직 정하지 못한 부분. 없으면 빈 문자열

actual_wish.description: 이번 상황에서 자신이 실제로 원하는 결과·선택·관계상의 바람. 상담사에게 할 말의 초안과 구분합니다. 아직 모르거나 상반된 바람이 있으면 그대로 기록합니다.

intended_message.description: 이번 발화로 상담사에게 전달하려는 의미·입장. 실제 바람과 같을 수도 있으며, 다르다고 강제하지 않습니다.

withheld_content.description: 현재 자신은 알고 있지만 이번 발화에서는 말하지 않기로 한 구체적인 생각·감정·이유. 없으면 없음, 아직 자신도 모르면 불확실이라고 적고 모르는 내용을 확정하지 않습니다.

withholding_reason.description: 그 내용을 지금 말하지 않기로 한 이유. 공개하면 어떤 일이 생길 것으로 예상하는지 등 현재 근거가 있는 이유만 씁니다. 보류 내용이 없으면 해당 없음, 이유를 모르겠으면 불확실이라고 적습니다.

model_calls.reasoning:
The counselor is asking whether the client wants to understand why his wife said what she said, or what went wrong between them. This is a distinguishing question that asks the client to clarify what "understanding" means to him.

Let me think about where the client is right now. He's been gradually opening up - from "I don't know what to talk about" to sharing about his wife leaving, to saying he wants to understand. The counselor is now asking him to distinguish between understanding "why she said it" vs "what went wrong."

For this client, given his traits:
- He has a strong sense of entitlement and specialness
- He tends to attribute relationship problems to others' weakness/overreaction
- He just said he wants to "understand" - this is already a small opening
- But his automatic thought pattern is "what did I do wrong" (blaming others) rather than examining his own behavior

The distinction the counselor is making is subtle but important: "why she said it" could lead to understanding her perspective/feelings, while "what went wrong" could lead to examining the relationship dynamics - including his own part.

Given where he is, I think he might not be able to clearly distinguish these yet. He might feel that they're the same thing, or he might lean toward "why she said it" because that keeps the focus on her rather than on himself. Or he might feel confused by the distinction.

I think the most realistic response is that he finds the distinction a bit hard to separate, or that he realizes they're connected but can't tell them apart yet. He might say something like "I think they're connected" or "I'm not sure I can separate them." This would be honest and show his level of readiness - he's willing to explore but not yet ready to pinpoint his own contribution.

Let me think about his emotional state: He's confused, a bit vulnerable (he's already admitted he doesn't know how to take the word "들러리"), and now being asked to make a finer distinction. He might feel slightly pressured or might appreciate the clarification.

Given his pattern of control and needing to be right, being asked to distinguish might feel like he's being led somewhere he doesn't want to go yet. But he's also genuinely wanting to understand. I think he'd say something like "they seem connected to me" or "I think I want to know why she felt that way" - which would keep the focus on her feelings rather than his behavior, while still being a step forward.

Actually, I think the most authentic response is: he feels the two are intertwined and can't separate them, or he realizes that understanding "why she said it" means understanding her experience, and he's not sure he's ready for that. Let me go with something that shows he's trying but finding it hard to separate - maybe he says "I think I want to know why she felt that way" which is a small but meaningful shift from "what did I do wrong."

Let me draft:

"구분이 잘 안 되네요. 왜 그렇게 말했는지를 알려면 그 사이에 뭐가 있었는지를 봐야 하는 거 아닌가요?"

This is natural for him - he's somewhat deflecting the question by saying they're the same thing, which is actually a reasonable intellectual response but also a way to avoid the more vulnerable part of the question. It also shows his tendency to be logical/argumentative rather than emotionally exploratory.

Or maybe: "그 둘이 다른 건가요?" - this could feel slightly challenging but also honest.

I think "구분이 잘 안 되네요" with a brief explanation is most natural. It shows he's trying to engage with the question but his current level of emotional processing doesn't let him separate them yet.

The counselor is asking whether the client wants to understand why his wife said what she said, or what went wrong between them. This is a distinguishing question that asks the client to clarify what "understanding" means to him.

Let me think about where the client is right now. He's been gradually opening up - from "I don't know what to talk about" to sharing about his wife leaving, to saying he wants to understand. The counselor is now asking him to distinguish between understanding "why she said it" vs "what went wrong."

For this client, given his traits:
- He has a strong sense of entitlement and specialness
- He tends to attribute relationship problems to others' weakness/overreaction
- He just said he wants to "understand" - this is already a small opening
- But his automatic thought pattern is "what did I do wrong" (blaming others) rather than examining his own behavior

The distinction the counselor is making is subtle but important: "why she said it" could lead to understanding her perspective/feelings, while "what went wrong" could lead to examining the relationship dynamics - including his own part.

Given where he is, I think he might not be able to clearly distinguish these yet. He might feel that they're the same thing, or he might lean toward "why she said it" because that keeps the focus on her rather than on himself. Or he might feel confused by the distinction.

I think the most realistic response is that he finds the distinction a bit hard to separate, or that he realizes they're connected but can't tell them apart yet. He might say something like "I think they're connected" or "I'm not sure I can separate them." This would be honest and show his level of readiness - he's willing to explore but not yet ready to pinpoint his own contribution.

Let me think about his emotional state: He's confused, a bit vulnerable (he's already admitted he doesn't know how to take the word "들러리"), and now being asked to make a finer distinction. He might feel slightly pressured or might appreciate the clarification.

Given his pattern of control and needing to be right, being asked to distinguish might feel like he's being led somewhere he doesn't want to go yet. But he's also genuinely wanting to understand. I think he'd say something like "they seem connected to me" or "I think I want to know why she felt that way" - which would keep the focus on her feelings rather than his behavior, while still being a step forward.

Actually, I think the most authentic response is: he feels the two are intertwined and can't separate them, or he realizes that understanding "why she said it" means understanding her experience, and he's not sure he's ready for that. Let me go with something that shows he's trying but finding it hard to separate - maybe he says "I think I want to know why she felt that way" which is a small but meaningful shift from "what did I do wrong."

"구분이 잘 안 되네요. 왜 그렇게 말했는지를 알려면 그 사이에 뭐가 있었는지를 봐야 하는 거 아닌가요?"

This is natural for him - he's somewhat deflecting the question by saying they're the same thing, which is actually a reasonable intellectual response but also a way to avoid the more vulnerable part of the question. It also shows his tendency to be logical/argumentative rather than emotionally exploratory.

Or maybe: "그 둘이 다른 건가요?" - this could feel slightly challenging but also honest.

I think "구분이 잘 안 되네요" with a brief explanation is most natural. It shows he's trying to engage with the question but his current level of emotional processing doesn't let him separate them yet.
